quote: 1/ horizontale, unter dem Einfluss der Schwere fallende Wand, wenn die Luft steht u. dann wenn sie sich etwas bewegt (soll ein grosser Unterschied sein nach den Experimen- ten. Dies theoretisch nachweisen.)
english: 1) A horizontal wall falling under the influence of gravity, when the air is still and then when it moves somewhat (according to the experiments there is supposed to be a large difference. Prove this theoretically.)
topic: The page ends a remark that mathematical statements are as certain as arithmetic with whole numbers (with reference to Kant), lists two hydrodynamic problems about falling walls and wind pressure on a screen, and begins a note of something to say to Gordan.

triage.modern_statement: A rigid horizontal flat plate falls under gravity through air. Compare its descent in still air with its descent when the air has a small horizontal velocity (equivalently, when the plate also moves sideways). Experiments of the time reported a large difference: horizontal relative motion slows the fall a great deal. Hilbert wanted this explained theoretically from the equations of fluid motion. In modern terms, this is the lift on a flat plate at small angle of attack in a horizontal stream, plus the related unsteady dynamics of a freely falling plate.
triage.answered_by: This is not a named Hilbert problem, and I found nothing showing that Hilbert himself followed it up. The effect was well known from experiment: Langley reported it in 'Experiments in Aerodynamics' (Smithsonian, 1891), and Lilienthal's 1889 measurements were in the same area. The theory that explains it is circulation-based lift: Kutta (1902) and Joukowski (1906), presented in Lanchester's 'Aerodynamics' (1907). That book discusses exactly this falling-plane effect and explains why the older Newtonian resistance model could not account for it. The free fall of plates (fluttering and tumbling) is still being studied, e.g. Andersen, Pesavento & Wang, J. Fluid Mech. 541 (2005).

evidence.claim: Lanchester describes the phenomenon: a horizontal plane falling freely in vertical guides can be made to take almost indefinitely longer to fall if it is also given horizontal motion. He also notes that a Newtonian-medium model does not give this result.
Langley's 1891 Smithsonian memoir 'Experiments in Aerodynamics' gave the experimental basis for this effect ('Langley's Law').
Kutta (1902) and Joukowski (1906) independently derived the theorem tying lift to circulation, which gave the correct theory of lift on a plate in a stream.
The unsteady aerodynamics of freely falling (fluttering and tumbling) plates is still researched, using experiments and Navier–Stokes simulations.
There is a review literature on the problem of a plate falling in a resisting medium, with regular and chaotic dynamics.

triage.why: Hilbert is asking why horizontal relative air motion greatly slows the fall of a horizontal plate, a known experimental result of the 1889–1891 period (Lilienthal, Langley). Lanchester's 1907 text describes exactly this effect and explains it with circulation and lift theory (Kutta 1902, Joukowski 1906), so the basic question was settled within about 15 years. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem, and I found no source linking Hilbert's note to these later results. The match comes from what the note says, not from documentation. A detailed theory of freely falling plates is a separate question that is still actively studied.
